Semarang is Central Java's capital, known for its Dutch colonial Old Town and the Lawang Sewu building of a 'thousand doors'.
Sendai is known as the 'City of Trees' and hosts the Tanabata star festival with huge paper streamers every August.
South Korea's capital sits on the Han River and is home to roughly a fifth of the country's population.
Seville's Giralda tower began life as the minaret of the Almohad mosque, and its bell was rung as a city alarm from the twelfth century on.
China's largest city sits on the Yangtze River Delta and hosts one of the world's busiest container ports.
Sharjah is the UAE's cultural capital, known for its museums and as the only emirate with coasts on both the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
Sheffield is known as the 'Steel City' and was where stainless steel was invented in 1913.
Shenyang holds the Mukden Palace, built by the Manchu rulers before they conquered Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty.
Shenzhen was a cluster of fishing villages until 1980, when it became China's first Special Economic Zone; it is now home to Huawei and Tencent.
Shigatse's Tashilhunpo Monastery, seat of the Panchen Lamas, holds China's largest gilded Buddha statue and stands across the Tsangpo River from the old town.
Shiraz is the Iranian city of poetry and gardens, and the nearby Pink Mosque glows with colored light through stained-glass windows.
Shymkent is Kazakhstan's third-largest city and lies on the ancient Silk Road near the Uzbek border.
The town is the base for visiting Angkor, just a few kilometres to the north.
Silkeborg is a Danish lakeside town whose museum displays the Tollund Man, a remarkably well-preserved Iron Age bog body.
This city-state at the tip of the Malay Peninsula is also its own sovereign country, one of only a few city-states left in the world.
This remote island off the coast of County Kerry, Ireland, was a Christian monastery from the 6th to 12th century and featured in Star Wars films.
Sofia stands on a cluster of mineral springs, and the Romans of Serdica heated their city and their baths with water drawn from the same springs.
Srinagar is the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, known for its Mughal gardens and houseboats on Dal Lake.
One of North America's oldest European-founded cities, its Signal Hill received Marconi's first transatlantic radio signal in 1901.
St. Louis is known as the Gateway to the West and played a major role in westward expansion.
Divers still leap from the Mostar bridge's 21-metre arch into the Neretva River in an annual competition.
Stockholm is spread across fourteen islands stitched together by around thirty bridges, which is why it is called the Venice of the North.
This Rhine city on the German border hosts the European Parliament and the European Court of Human Rights.
Stuttgart is the birthplace of the car and home to both Mercedes-Benz and Porsche.
Suez is the port at the southern end of the Suez Canal, where the canal meets the Red Sea.
Sulaymaniyah is a city in Iraqi Kurdistan known as a center of Kurdish culture, poetry, and the arts.
Surabaya is Indonesia's second-largest city and is known as the 'City of Heroes' for its 1945 battle against British forces.
Surat is the world's diamond-cutting capital, where most of the world's rough diamonds are cut and polished.
Surrey is a fast-growing city in Metro Vancouver and is set to become British Columbia's largest city.
Fiji's capital sits on a peninsula on the island of Viti Levu and is one of the wettest capitals on Earth.
Suwon is home to the Hwaseong Fortress, built in the 1790s by King Jeongjo, and is famous for its marinated galbi ribs.
Suzhou is the 'Venice of the East,' with canals and UNESCO-listed classical gardens, and has been a silk center for centuries.
Australia's most populous city is built around the drowned river valley of Port Jackson.
Tabriz has one of the oldest covered bazaars in the world and is a historic center of Persian carpet weaving.
Taichung is Taiwan's second-largest city, where bubble tea is said to have been invented in the 1980s.
Tainan is Taiwan's oldest city and former capital, packed with temples and known as the island's street-food capital.
Taipei is famous for its night markets and the National Palace Museum, which holds a vast collection of Chinese imperial treasures.
Taiz is a city in Yemen's southern highlands, located below the mountain of Jabal Sabir, and is a historic center of learning.
Takeo is a Cambodian provincial town near Phnom Da, an ancient temple from the pre-Angkor era.
Tallinn's Old Town is a walled Hanseatic city left so intact that its town hall square doubles as an ice rink every winter.
Tambacounda is a Senegalese town on the Dakar–Niger railway and the gateway to Niokolo-Koba National Park.
Its Ybor City district was built by Cuban and Spanish immigrants and once rolled hundreds of millions of cigars a year.
Tangier sits at the Strait of Gibraltar, where Africa is just 14 km from Europe, and once had international-zone status.
South Tarawa is Kiribati's capital and is one of the most densely populated places in the Pacific.
Tarkwa is a Ghanaian gold-mining town with some of the largest gold mines in West Africa.
Tashkent is Uzbekistan's capital and the largest city in Central Asia, with a famous Chorsu Bazaar under a giant blue dome.
Tbilisi is Georgia's capital, known for its sulfur bathhouses, balconied old town, and a long winemaking tradition.
Tegucigalpa is Honduras's mountain capital, and its airport is known for one of the world's trickiest landing approaches.
Tehran is Iran's capital and has one of the world's largest bazaars, along with a museum holding the Crown Jewels.
Founded beside ancient Jaffa in 1909, it is known for beaches, nightlife, and thousands of Bauhaus-style buildings.
The Netherlands' seat of government isn't its capital, and it hosts the International Court of Justice in the Peace Palace.
Greece's second city is named after Alexander the Great's half-sister, and its seafront is marked by the White Tower.
Bhutan's capital has no traffic lights, directed instead by white-gloved officers, and is one of the few capitals without them.
Tianjin is the port gateway to Beijing and keeps a waterfront of old foreign concession buildings from its days as a treaty port.
Tijuana is a border city next to San Diego and is often credited as the birthplace of the Caesar salad.
Tiksi is a remote Arctic port in Yakutia, Russia, located on the shore of the Laptev Sea.
This Malian city flourished in the 14th century as a center of gold, salt, and Islamic scholarship, home to thousands of ancient manuscripts.
Japan's capital is the world's most populous metropolitan area, sprawled across 23 special wards on Honshu.
Historic city with Jewish quarter.
Tomsk is a Siberian university city known for its ornate wooden houses decorated with carved lace-like designs.
Toronto is Canada's largest city and is often ranked among the most multicultural cities in the world.
Touba is the holy city of Senegal's Mouride Sufi brotherhood, whose yearly Grand Magal draws millions of pilgrims.
Nicknamed 'la Ville Rose' for its pink brick, it is the home of Airbus and Europe's aerospace industry.
Libya's capital and largest city, founded by the Phoenicians in the 7th century BCE as Oea.
A cliff formed when a glacier's rockfall hit the valley wall, the tongue's name comes from trolls supposedly using it as a lookout.
Known as the Gateway to the Arctic, Tromsø is located above the Arctic Circle in Norway and is a prime location to view the Northern Lights.
Troy is an ancient city in northwest Asia Minor.
Trujillo is near Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas, and is the home of Peru's marinera dance.
Ringed by the giant saguaro cacti of the Sonoran Desert, it also has an aircraft boneyard holding thousands of retired military planes.
Tunisia's capital sits at the edge of Lake Tunis and is known for its historic medina, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Turin gave the world the Fiat 500, launched here as the tiny Topolino in 1957, and its automobile museum grew from the car collection of the first House of Savoy.
The white City Palace, still home to the Mewar royal family after four centuries, overlooks Lake Pichola, an artificial island made by damming a valley in the 14th century.
The coldest national capital on Earth, it began as a mobile Buddhist monastic center before settling permanently in 1778.
Ulsan is South Korea's industrial powerhouse, home to Hyundai's huge car factory and shipyard.
Ürümqi is Xinjiang's capital and is often cited as the city farthest from any ocean on Earth.
The waterfront sign celebrates Ushuaia's claim as the world's southernmost city. The Beagle Channel and Martial Mountains frame the setting.
The capital of this tiny Alpine microstate is overlooked by a castle still owned by the ruling prince's family.
Vagator is a beach in North Goa, overlooked by the ruins of Chapora Fort.
Valencia is the birthplace of paella and hosts Las Fallas, a festival where giant papier-mâché figures are burned.
The Knights of St John built this compact walled capital after surviving a sixteenth-century siege.
This funicular climbs between the port district and Paseo 21 de Mayo. It is one of the city's historic hillside elevators.
Lake Ercek sits nearly 1,190 m above sea level beside the city, and the Urartian citadel of Toprakkale still stands on a rock just offshore.
Vancouver is consistently ranked among the world's most livable cities and is surrounded by mountains and ocean.
Varanasi is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, and Hindus believe dying there brings release from the cycle of rebirth.
This Italian city has no roads, only canals and footbridges linking its 118 small islands.
Veracruz was Mexico's first Spanish port, founded by Hernán Cortés in 1519, and is known for its lively carnival.
Grand government buildings and gardens give this Pacific island capital a strong British character.
Once the seat of the Habsburg Empire, this city has topped global liveability rankings for years running.
Vientiane is the laid-back capital of Laos on the Mekong River, home to the golden Pha That Luang stupa.
Largest medieval old town in Eastern Europe.
Vinh is a Vietnamese city near the birthplace of Ho Chi Minh and was rebuilt with East German help after the war.
Visakhapatnam is a port city in Andhra Pradesh with a decommissioned submarine turned museum on its beachfront.
A Soviet decree kept foreigners out until 1992, and the city's terminus anchors the 9,289 km Trans-Siberian Railway, the longest in the world.
Volgograd, formerly Stalingrad, was the site of the decisive WWII battle and is watched over by the colossal Motherland Calls statue.
After 1944 the Nazis blew up about 85% of Warsaw and left it standing in ruins, so almost everything you see today was rebuilt brick by brick.
The U.S. capital was designed by Pierre Charles L'Enfant and is located along the Potomac River.
Wellington is the windiest capital city in the world, with an average wind speed of 27 km/h.
Whitehorse is the capital of Yukon Territory and was a key hub during the Klondike Gold Rush.
Germany ruled the territory until 1915, and the city's Lutheran Christuskirche dates from 1910.
Winnipeg is at the meeting of the Red and Assiniboine rivers and gave its name to the bear that inspired Winnie-the-Pooh.
Wrocław is a Polish city of bridges and islands, famous for the hundreds of small bronze dwarf statues around town.
Wuhan sits where the Han River joins the Yangtze, and its Yellow Crane Tower is one of China's most celebrated historic towers.
Xiamen is a Fujian port city whose car-free Gulangyu islet is known for colonial villas and a strong piano culture.
Xi'an was the capital of thirteen dynasties and the eastern terminus of the Silk Road, whose worn paving stones still surface in the city.
Xining sits on the edge of the Tibetan Plateau at about 2,200 meters and is the gateway to Qinghai Lake and the Kumbum Monastery.
Yangon is Myanmar's largest city and is famous for its many British colonial buildings.
Yantai is a Shandong port on the Bohai Strait and one of China's oldest wine regions, home to the Changyu winery founded in 1892.
Yaoundé is Cameroon's capital, built on seven hills in the country's forested south.
This is the de facto capital of Nauru, the world's third-smallest country, an island once stripped bare by phosphate mining.
Yaroslavl is one of the oldest cities on the Volga and part of Russia's Golden Ring of historic towns.
Yazd is an Iranian desert city famous for its badgir wind towers and an eternal flame said to have burned since AD 470.
Yekaterinburg is where the last tsar, Nicholas II, and his family were executed in 1918, and it sits on the border of Europe and Asia.
Yellowknife is the capital of the Northwest Territories and is known for its aurora borealis displays.
Yerevan is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, founded in 782 BC as the fortress of Erebuni.
Yichang is a Hubei city on the Yangtze next to the Three Gorges Dam, the world's largest hydroelectric power station.
Yokohama was one of the first Japanese ports opened to foreign trade in 1859 and has Japan's largest Chinatown.
Zagreb's Upper Town clings to a volcanic hill, and its Gri cannon has fired one blank charge every New Year's Eve since 1815 to scare off bad spirits.
Zaječar is a Serbian town near Felix Romuliana, a UNESCO-listed Roman palace built by Emperor Galerius.
Zamboanga City is known as 'Asia's Latin City' because many residents speak Chavacano, a Spanish-based creole.
This Indian Ocean island's Stone Town was a hub of the 19th-century spice and slave trade under Omani Arab rule.
Zaragoza is a city on the Ebro famous for the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar and the Moorish Aljafería Palace.
Zaranj is the capital of Afghanistan's Nimruz province, on the border with Iran.
This car-free Alpine village sits at the foot of the Matterhorn, reachable only by train.
Zhengzhou is Henan's capital and a key rail crossroads, located near the Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
Zurich ranks as the most expensive city on earth by cost of living, and its Bahnhofstrasse was lit by electric lamps before almost any other street in Europe.
Colombia's capital sits at 2,640 meters in the Andes, making it one of the world's highest capitals.
Tirana's drab communist-era apartment blocks were repainted in bright colors and geometric patterns starting in the early 2000s, a project led by then-mayor (and future prime minister) Edi Rama.
Andorra la Vella is the highest capital city in Europe, tucked into a steep valley of the Pyrenees between France and Spain.
St. John's harbor fills with cruise ships for most of the tourist season, and its colorful colonial-era warehouses along Redcliffe Quay once stored sugar, rum, and enslaved people.
Nassau was a notorious pirate haven in the early 1700s and served as Blackbeard's base of operations before the British cracked down and turned it into a proper colonial capital.
Manama's twin Bahrain World Trade Center towers were the first skyscrapers in the world built with large wind turbines integrated directly into the structure to help power the building.
Bridgetown's historic Garrison district is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, laid out by British colonists around a bridge that the Indigenous Kalinago people had built across a swampy inlet.
Part of the city, Kampong Ayer, is a sprawling stilt village built over the Brunei River that's been continuously inhabited for over a thousand years, earning it the nickname Venice of the East.
Praia's historic center sits atop a flat volcanic plateau called the Platô, ringed by cliffs that long made the site easy to defend against pirate raids.
Moroni sits in the shadow of Mount Karthala, one of the world's largest active volcanoes, which has erupted more than twenty times since the 1800s.

San José's ornate National Theatre was built in the 1890s after European opera companies skipped Costa Rica for lack of a proper venue, funded by a tax that coffee growers paid on every bag they exported.
Nicosia is the world's last divided capital, split since 1974 by a UN-patrolled buffer zone known as the Green Line that still cuts straight through the old city.
Despite its small size, Djibouti simultaneously hosts military bases from the US, France, Japan, and China, all drawn by the city's position next to one of the world's busiest shipping chokepoints.
Roseau is the gateway to the Boiling Lake, the world's second-largest hot spring, a flooded fumarole hidden deep in Dominica's rainforest.
Malabo sits not on Equatorial Guinea's mainland but on Bioko Island, over 150 kilometers offshore, inside the caldera of an extinct volcano.
Mbabane handles the government paperwork but isn't Eswatini's only capital: royal and legislative affairs happen a few kilometers away in Lobamba, the country's traditional seat of the monarchy.
Banjul is built on a small island at the mouth of the Gambia River and was founded in 1816 as a British naval base to intercept Atlantic slave ships.
St. George's horseshoe-shaped harbor, known as the Carenage, is often called one of the prettiest in the Caribbean, ringed by pastel warehouses built into the hillside.
Bissau's old fortress, the Fortaleza d'Amura, holds the mausoleum of Amílcar Cabral, the independence leader assassinated in 1973, a year before Guinea-Bissau broke from Portugal.
Much of Georgetown sits below sea level and is protected by a Dutch-built sea wall and a network of drainage canals, a legacy of Guyana's early Dutch colonizers.
Kuwait City's skyline is anchored by the Kuwait Towers, water towers shaped like giant skewered balls that have been the country's national symbol since opening in 1979.
Maseru sits right on the border of South Africa, which surrounds landlocked Lesotho entirely, and grew up around a police camp established on the Caledon River in 1869.
Port Louis is home to the Champ de Mars, the oldest horse-racing track in the Southern Hemisphere, which has hosted races continuously since 1812.
Podgorica was renamed Titograd in 1946 in honor of Yugoslav leader Josip Broz Tito and kept that name until Montenegro restored the city's original name in 1992.

A massive earthquake leveled much of Skopje in 1963, and decades later the government responded with 'Skopje 2014,' a controversial building spree that covered downtown in neoclassical facades and dozens of new statues.
Basseterre's harbor was a key hub of the Caribbean sugar and slave trade in the 1600s and 1700s, and the island's old plantation railway, now a tourist train, still loops past the former cane fields.

clue: Kingstown, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines 🇻🇨

San Marino's three medieval fortress towers perched on Monte Titano have watched over the country since the 11th century, and the republic claims to be the oldest sovereign state in the world, founded in 301 AD.

clue: São Tomé, Sao Tome and Principe 🇸🇹
fact: São Tomé sits almost exactly on the equator, and the island's old Portuguese cocoa plantations, called roças, once made the country one of the world's largest cocoa producers.
Victoria's landmark clock tower is a miniature replica of one that used to stand near London's Vauxhall Bridge, erected in 1903 to mark Seychelles becoming a separate British colony.
Juba sits on the banks of the White Nile and became the capital of the world's newest country when South Sudan gained independence from Sudan in 2011.

Paramaribo has a mosque and a Hindu temple standing directly next to each other downtown, a landmark often cited as a symbol of Suriname's unusually diverse mix of Creole, Javanese, Hindustani, and Dutch heritage.

clue: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago 🇹🇹
fact: Port of Spain is the birthplace of the steelpan, invented in the city's streets in the 1930s and '40s when locals began tuning discarded oil drums, and it still hosts one of the world's biggest Carnival celebrations.
Montevideo's Estadio Centenario hosted the first-ever FIFA World Cup final in 1930, which Uruguay won on home soil.

Belmopan became Belize's capital in 1970 after the former capital, Belize City, was devastated by Hurricane Hattie. It is one of the world's smallest national capitals and sits near the geographic center of the country.
Castries is Saint Lucia's capital and main port, built around a sheltered harbor on the island's northwest coast. The city was largely rebuilt on a grid after a devastating fire in 1948.
Funchal is the capital of Madeira and sits on the island's sunny south coast. Its steep streets descend toward a busy Atlantic harbor.
Gdansk is a historic Baltic port whose Main Town was rebuilt after the devastation of World War II. It is also the birthplace of the Solidarity movement.
Krakow was Poland's royal capital until 1596 and remains one of the country's leading cultural and academic centers. Its Main Market Square is one of Europe's largest medieval squares.
Stavanger is a port city on Norway's southwest coast and a gateway to the Lysefjord and Preikestolen. It grew from a historic fishing and canning center into Norway's petroleum capital.
Ljubljana is Slovenia's capital, centered on the Ljubljanica River beneath a hilltop medieval castle. Its compact center is known for bridges, riverside cafés, and car-free streets.

Bolivia's declaration of independence was signed here in 1825, in the Casa de la Libertad. Just outside town, a quarry wall at Cal Orck'o holds thousands of dinosaur footprints, tilted almost vertical by mountain-building.
Burundi moved its political capital here from lakeside Bujumbura in 2019. The drum sanctuary at nearby Gishora keeps alive the royal drumming ritual UNESCO listed in 2014.
President Félix Houphouët-Boigny turned his home village into the capital and built the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, modeled on St. Peter's in Rome. Pope John Paul II consecrated it in 1990.
Yasser Arafat is buried in a stone mausoleum inside the Muqata'a compound, and the poet Mahmoud Darwish lies in a hilltop museum garden across town.

Lima almost never gets real rain, yet spends winter under a grey sea fog called garúa. In Miraflores, the adobe pyramid of Huaca Pucllana rises between apartment blocks, built centuries before the Inca.
Einstein worked out special relativity in 1905 while living at Kramgasse 49, steps from the Zytglogge clock tower. The city keeps live bears in a riverside park, a nod to its name.
Ashgabat holds the Guinness record for the most white-marble-clad buildings of any city, over 500 of them. Nearly the whole city had to be rebuilt after a 1948 earthquake flattened it.
The world's smallest country covers about 44 hectares and is protected by the Swiss Guard, which has served the pope since 1506.
Gaudí's Sagrada Família, under construction since 1882, rises over the grid-planned Eixample district. The city hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics.
The four-minaret Charminar, built in 1591, anchors Hyderabad's old city. Once the great trading centre for Golconda diamonds, it is now a major IT hub nicknamed Cyberabad.
Medellín opened Colombia's first metro in 1995 and links its steep hillside neighbourhoods to it with cable cars. Its mild climate earned it the nickname City of Eternal Spring.
Cusco was the capital of the Inca Empire, and Spanish colonial churches were built directly on its fitted Inca stone walls. It is the main gateway for travellers heading to Machu Picchu.
La Paz is Bolivia's seat of government, while Sucre is the constitutional capital. Its Mi Teleférico network is the largest urban cable-car system in the world.
Fortaleza takes its name from a 17th-century Dutch fort later taken over by the Portuguese. Its beachfront Avenida Beira-Mar hosts a craft fair every night.
Yogyakarta is the only Indonesian region still governed by a hereditary sultan, whose Kraton palace sits at the city's heart. The temples of Borobudur and Prambanan lie nearby.
Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for nearly a thousand years, and grassy royal burial mounds still rise between its streets. Bulguksa Temple and Seokguram Grotto stand on its outskirts.
A 25-mile Greenbelt path follows the Boise River through the city. Its Basque Block celebrates one of the largest Basque communities in the United States.
Oklahoma City was settled almost overnight in the Land Run of April 22, 1889. Working oil wells stand on the grounds of the state capitol.
The dome of the Iowa State Capitol is covered in 23-karat gold leaf. Every August the city hosts the Iowa State Fair, famous for its life-size butter cow.
In 1957 federal troops escorted nine Black students into Little Rock Central High School during a landmark desegregation crisis. The city is also home to the Clinton Presidential Library.
Buffalo-style chicken wings were first served at the city's Anchor Bar in 1964. Niagara Falls lies a short drive to the north.
No roads connect Juneau to the rest of North America, so Alaska's capital is reached only by sea or air. The Mendenhall Glacier flows down to the edge of the city.
Spokane hosted Expo '74, the first world's fair with an environmental theme, beside the Spokane Falls. Riverfront Park now occupies the fairgrounds.
Roger Williams founded Providence in 1636 as a haven for religious freedom. In summer, WaterFire lights bonfires on the rivers running through downtown.
Founded by the Romans as Lugdunum where the Rhône meets the Saône, it later became Europe's silk-weaving capital.
